title: Finite generation inside a free Frobenius skew-polynomial module implies freeness
statement:
Let $k$ be a field of prime characteristic $p>0$ [def-weil-field]. Define $A=k_\sigma[F]$, where $\sigma(c)=c^p$, to be the ring of finite sums $\sum_{i\geq0}c_iF^i$ with coefficientwise addition and multiplication
$$(aF^i)(bF^j)=a b^{p^i}F^{i+j}.$$
Let $I$ be any set and let $A^{(I)}$ denote the left $A$-module of finitely supported families $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ with coordinatewise addition and left multiplication. If $M\subseteq A^{(I)}$ is a left $A$-submodule generated by finitely many elements [def-weil-finitely-generated-module], then there exist $d\geq0$ and an isomorphism of left $A$-modules $A^d\xrightarrow{\sim}M$. A left submodule is an additive subgroup closed under left multiplication by every element of $A$, and a module isomorphism is an additive bijection respecting this multiplication. No perfectness hypothesis is imposed on $k$. The empty index set and the zero submodule are allowed.

source.place: Proposition 14.50 and the preceding division algorithm, printed p.296; its finite-support application in the elementary-unipotent case of Theorem 16.58, printed p.345. The arbitrary free ambient module reduces to finitely many coordinates because M is finitely generated.

proof.text: Choose finitely many generators $m_1,\ldots,m_t$ of $M$, using [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Let $J\subseteq I$ be the union of their finite supports. Left multiplication acts coordinatewise, so every $\sum_j a_jm_j$ is supported on $J$. Thus restriction to $J$ and extension by zero identify $M$ with a submodule of $A^n$, where $n=|J|$. If $J$ is empty then $M=0$.

proof.text: Every left ideal $L\subseteq A$ is principal. For $L=0$ take the generator $0$. Otherwise choose a nonzero $g\in L$ of least degree. For $f\in L$, [lem-sfb-frobenius-skew-left-multiple-division] gives $f=qg+r$ with $r=0$ or $\deg r<\deg g$. Since $L$ is closed under left multiplication, $r=f-qg\in L$. Minimality excludes a nonzero $r$, so $L=Ag$. Only division with $q$ on the left has been used.

source.place: Proposition 14.50 and its preceding division algorithm, printed p.296; finite-support application in Theorem 16.58, printed p.345. The coordinate induction expands the polynomial-ring comparison left unproved in Proposition 14.50.

proof.text: Prove by induction on $n$ that EVERY left submodule $N\subseteq A^n$ has a finite basis of size at most $n$; finite generation is not required for this inductive claim. At $n=0$, $N=0$ has the empty basis. For $n>0$, let $\pi:N\to A$ be first-coordinate projection. Its image $L$ is an additive subgroup closed under left multiplication, hence a left ideal. Put $K=\ker\pi$. Deleting the zero first coordinate identifies $K$ with a submodule of $A^{n-1}$, so by the induction hypothesis $K$ has a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_e$ with $e\leq n-1$.

source.place: Proposition 14.50 and its preceding division algorithm, printed p.296; finite-support application in Theorem 16.58, printed p.345. The coordinate induction expands the polynomial-ring comparison left unproved in Proposition 14.50.

proof.text: If $L=0$, then $N=K$ and that basis suffices. Otherwise step 3 gives $L=Ag$ with $g\ne0$; choose $x\in N$ with $\pi(x)=g$. Every $y\in N$ has $\pi(y)=ag$ for some $a\in A$, whence $y-ax\in K$, so $x,v_1,\ldots,v_e$ span $N$. A relation $ax+\sum_i b_i v_i=0$ gives $ag=0$ in the first coordinate, so step 2 forces $a=0$, and independence of the $v_i$ forces every $b_i=0$. Thus the map $(a,b_1,\ldots,b_e)\mapsto ax+\sum_i b_i v_i$ is a left-linear bijection $A^{e+1}\to N$. This closes the induction. Applying it to the submodule obtained in step 1 yields the claimed isomorphism with finite $d$; the empty basis yields $d=0$ for the zero submodule.
